## 1.  Goal of the adversarial test  

The purpose of the test is **not** to prove that the app works (that is what a well‑designed RCT would do) but to **stress‑test** the hospital’s observational claim that “using the app *causes* a 40 % reduction in readmission”.  
An *adversarial* design deliberately looks for hidden biases, omitted variables, and alternative mechanisms that could generate the same association without a true causal effect.

---

## 2.  Core design: “What‑If‑We‑Had‑Randomisation” + Robustness checks  

| Step | What we do | Why it helps expose a flaw |
|------|------------|----------------------------|
| **A. Create a synthetic “randomised‑like” cohort** | Using the existing data, apply **propensity‑score matching (PSM)**, **coarsened exact matching (CEM)** or **inverse‑probability‑weighting (IPW)** to balance every observable characteristic between app users and non‑users (age, gender, comorbidities, severity scores, insurance type, previous utilization, socioeconomic status, digital‑literacy proxies, etc.). | If the 40 % gap disappears (or shrinks dramatically) after balancing, the original association was driven by confounding rather than causation. |
| **B. Instrumental‑Variable (IV) “natural experiment”** | Identify an exogenous source of variation that influences *whether a patient uses the app* but is unrelated to health status—e.g., **appointment‑time slot of the discharge education session** (some nurses hand out QR‑codes only during certain shifts), **availability of a bedside tablet** (some wards have them, others do not), or **geographic variation in Wi‑Fi coverage**. Use this as an IV to estimate the **Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE)** of the app. | If the IV estimate is far smaller (or non‑significant) than the naïve 40 % reduction, the original claim likely suffers from omitted‑variable bias. |
| **C. Difference‑in‑Differences (DiD) with a rollout “staggered adoption”** | If the app was introduced ward‑by‑ward or month‑by‑month, compare readmission trends **before vs. after** introduction **within** each ward and **against** wards that have not yet received the app. Include ward‑level fixed effects and time trends. | A DiD that shows no differential drop in readmission after the app’s introduction (or a drop that predates the rollout) suggests the observed association is spurious. |
| **D. Sensitivity‑analysis / Rosenbaum bounds** | After matching, compute how strong an unobserved confounder would need to be to erase the observed effect (e.g., using the **Rosenbaum sensitivity** package). | If a modest hidden bias could overturn the result, the causal claim is fragile. |
| **E. “Placebo” outcome and “placebo” treatment** | Choose an outcome that should *not* be affected by the app (e.g., **rate of elective orthopedic surgery within 30 days**). Also, create a “fake” treatment variable (e.g., whether the patient’s discharge paperwork was printed in colour). Test the association. | A significant “effect” on a placebo outcome or with a placebo treatment indicates systematic bias (e.g., data‑collection artifacts). |
| **F. Time‑lag analysis** | Examine whether the reduction in readmission appears **immediately** after discharge or only after a certain lag (e.g., >30 days). | A causal effect of an app that mainly provides medication reminders should appear early; a delayed effect may hint at a confounding factor that evolves over time (e.g., better follow‑up care). |
| **G. Sub‑group falsification** | Test the effect in sub‑populations that cannot plausibly benefit from the app (e.g., **patients with severe cognitive impairment** who cannot use a smartphone). | If the same 40 % reduction shows up in this group, the association is unlikely to be caused by the app. |

**Adversarial “pass/fail” rule:**  
- **Fail** if any of the above robustness checks reduces the estimated effect to <10 % (or makes it statistically non‑significant).  
- **Pass** only if the effect remains statistically and clinically robust across *all* checks, indicating that the original claim survived a battery of stress tests.

---

## 3.  Data requirements for the adversarial test  

| Data element | Reason |
|--------------|--------|
| **Patient‑level clinical data** – diagnosis codes, Elixhauser/Charlson comorbidity scores, severity indices, lab values, vital signs at discharge. | Controls for health status. |
| **Utilisation history** – prior admissions, ED visits, outpatient follow‑up attendance. | Captures habitual health‑care users. |
| **Socio‑demographic variables** – age, sex, race/ethnicity, zip‑code, insurance type, income proxy, education level, language. | Adjusts for social determinants and digital‑access gaps. |
| **Digital‑literacy / device access proxies** – whether a patient owns a smartphone, broadband availability in zip‑code, prior portal log‑ins. | Directly addresses selection into app use. |
| **Process variables** – nurse who performed discharge education, shift, ward, availability of bedside tablet, discharge checklist version. | Needed for constructing an IV or staggered rollout indicator. |
| **Outcome variables** – 30‑day all‑cause readmission (primary), 30‑day readmission for specific conditions (secondary), placebo outcomes (elective surgery, trauma visits). | Allows primary and falsification tests. |
| **Time stamps** – exact discharge time, app‑first‑login time, date of any app‑generated alerts. | Enables lag analysis. |
| **Hospital‑level variables** – staffing ratios, ward occupancy, seasonal flu activity, hospital policy changes. | Controls for macro‑level confounders. |

All data should be extracted from the **electronic health record (EHR)** and the **mobile‑app analytics platform** under a secure, IRB‑approved protocol.

**The Counterfactual in Question**

> “If my AI lawyer had told me to take the plea deal, I wouldn’t be in prison.”

This is a *counterfactual conditional* of the form  

\[
\text{If } p \text{ had been true, then } q \text{ would have been true},
\]

where  

* **p** = *the AI lawyer’s advice was “take the plea deal”*  
* **q** = *the defendant would not be in prison*.

For a counterfactual of this shape to be meaningful, a number of logical, semantic, and causal conditions must be satisfied. Below is a step‑by‑step analysis of those requirements, expressed in the language of contemporary counterfactual theory (Lewis‑Stalnaker possible‑world semantics) and causal‑model theory (Pearl’s structural equations).

---

## 1. A Well‑Formed Counterfactual Needs a *Causal Model*

A counterfactual is not just a linguistic curiosity; it presupposes a **causal structure** that connects the antecedent (*p*) to the consequent (*q*). In a structural‑causal model (SCM) we would write something like:

```
AI_Advice  →  Defendant_Decision  →  Plea_Accepted  →  Conviction_Outcome  →  In_Prison
```

Each arrow represents a direct causal influence. The variables can be formalized as:

| Variable | Description | Type |
|----------|-------------|------|
| **A** (AI_Advice) | The recommendation the AI gives (take plea vs go to trial) | binary |
| **D** (Defendant_Decision) | Whether the defendant follows the AI’s recommendation | binary |
| **P** (Plea_Accepted) | Whether the prosecutor accepts the plea deal offered | binary |
| **C** (Conviction_Outcome) | The legal result (guilty‑trial, guilty‑plea, acquittal) | categorical |
| **J** (In_Prison) | Whether the defendant ends up incarcerated | binary |

The counterfactual “If A = *take‑plea* then J = 0” is meaningful only if there exists a **causal pathway** from *A* to *J* that is not blocked by intervening variables that are held fixed.

---

## 2. The Antecedent Must Be *Intervenable* (Manipulable)

In the language of Pearl, a counterfactual is evaluated by **intervening** on the model: we replace the structural equation for *A* with the value “take‑plea”. This is denoted `do(A = take‑plea)`. For the intervention to be legitimate:

1. **A is a genuine decision variable** – the AI could, in principle, have issued either recommendation.  
2. **The intervention does not violate logical impossibility** – the AI’s advice could have been different without contradicting the facts about the case (e.g., the plea deal actually existed).  

If the AI’s advice is *deterministically* forced by the facts (e.g., the AI is a deterministic function of the evidence, and that evidence makes the plea the only rational recommendation), then the antecedent is *counterfactually impossible*—the counterfactual would be vacuous because no possible world exists where the AI says otherwise while all other facts stay the same.

---

## 3. The Counterfactual Must Refer to the *Closest* Possible Worlds

Lewis‑Stalnaker semantics defines the truth of a counterfactual by looking at the **set of possible worlds** that are *closest* to the actual world while satisfying the antecedent. “Closest” is a similarity ordering that respects:

* **Minimal change** – keep as many facts as possible identical to the actual world, only altering what is forced by the antecedent.
* **Causal coherence** – changes must propagate through the causal model, not arbitrarily.

Thus, for the claim to have meaning we must be able to identify a world **W\*** such that:

1. In **W\***, **A = take‑plea** (the antecedent holds).  
2. All other variables that are *not* causally downstream of **A** stay as they are in the actual world (e.g., the evidence, the prosecutor’s discretion, the judge’s sentencing guidelines).  
3. The downstream variables **D**, **P**, **C**, **J** are recomputed according to the structural equations under the intervention `do(A = take‑plea)`.

If no such *closest* world exists—because, for instance, the plea would never have been offered, or the prosecutor would have rejected any plea—then the counterfactual is *undefined* or *trivially false*.

---

## 4. The Causal Chain Must Be *Sufficient* for the Consequent

Even after the intervention, we need to verify that the downstream chain **actually leads** to the desired outcome (**J = 0**). This requires several sub‑conditions:

| Sub‑condition | What it demands |
|---------------|-----------------|
| **D1 (Compliance)** | The defendant would have followed the AI’s advice (i.e., **D = follow‑advice**). |
| **P1 (Plea Availability)** | A viable plea bargain existed that the prosecutor would have accepted (**P = accepted**). |
| **C1 (Sentencing)** | The plea bargain’s recommended sentence did **not** include prison time (or included a sentence below the threshold for incarceration). |
| **J1 (No Prison)** | Given the plea’s sentence, the legal system would not have placed the defendant in prison (e.g., probation, fine, or dismissal). |

If any of these links fail, the counterfactual “If A = take‑plea then J = 0” is **false** in the closest possible world. For the claim to be *meaningful* (i.e., not trivially false), the defendant must plausibly have:

* Had the *capacity* to accept the plea (no mandatory trial clause).  
* Had *incentive* to follow the advice (no overriding personal or strategic reason to reject it).  
* Been *eligible* for a non‑prison sentence under the plea (the law permits a non‑custodial disposition for the offense).  

---

## 5. No *Confounding* or *Overdetermination* That Breaks the Counterfactual

A well‑behaved counterfactual requires that the antecedent **actually matters** for the consequent. Two technical threats:

1. **Confounding** – Some third factor **U** (e.g., the strength of the evidence) simultaneously determines both the AI’s advice and the likelihood of a prison sentence. If **U** is held constant across worlds, the counterfactual may still be meaningful, but we must acknowledge that the AI’s advice is only a *proxy* for **U**, not an independent cause.

2. **Overdetermination** – Even if the AI had advised a plea, an independent factor (say, a mandatory minimum statute) would have forced a prison term regardless of the plea. Below is a step‑by‑step narrative that links **the original historical record‑keeping practices** to the **real‑world discriminatory outcomes** observed after the model went live.  At each stage I note the decisions (or omissions) that acted as *causal levers* and I flag where an **intervention** could have broken the chain.

---

### 1. Historical Data Collection  

| What actually happened | Why it mattered for bias | Causal link to later stages |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **a. Redlining & “neighbourhood‑based” underwriting** – For decades the bank’s legacy scoring system used zip‑code, property value, and “community risk” metrics that were calibrated on a *segregated* housing market.  Minority‑dense zip codes systematically received lower credit limits or were denied outright. | The raw outcome variable (“loan repaid / default”) is already *biased*: many defaults in those zip codes were not caused by borrower behaviour but by under‑investment, higher rent‑to‑income ratios, or predatory lending. | The model later learns that *being in a certain zip code* → *higher probability of default*, even though the causal driver is structural discrimination, not individual creditworthiness. |
| **b. Missing or sparse data for protected groups** – Credit histories for many members of the minority group were thin (e.g., more cash‑only transactions, fewer traditional bank accounts). | The training set over‑represents “no‑history” or “thin‑file” borrowers from the minority group, which are often labeled “high risk” by default. | The model will treat *absence of data* as a risk signal, amplifying the disparity. |
| **c. Legacy “manual” decisions encoded as labels** – Human underwriters, who were themselves biased (consciously or unconsciously), over‑rode algorithmic recommendations for minority applicants and recorded them as “approved” or “rejected”. | The label (approved vs. rejected) already carries human bias. | The supervised learning algorithm is trained to reproduce those biased decisions. |

#### **Intervention Point #1 – Data Auditing & Re‑balancing (pre‑training)**  
*What could have been done*:  

1. **Bias audit of the historical loan file** – compare approval/denial rates, default rates, and loan terms across protected vs. non‑protected groups *controlling for income, employment, etc.*  
2. **Counterfactual re‑labeling** – replace biased outcomes with *de‑biased* targets (e.g., use “ability‑to‑repay” estimates from a separate, unbiased source, or simulate what the default rate *would have been* absent redlining).  
3. **Statistical parity re‑sampling** – over‑sample under‑represented high‑quality minority borrowers and under‑sample over‑represented low‑quality majority borrowers, or apply **importance weighting** that reflects the true population risk rather than the biased historical risk.  

*Effect*: The training distribution would no longer encode the legacy redlining signal, breaking the first causal link.

---

### 2. Feature Engineering Decisions  

| What actually happened | Why it mattered for bias | Causal link to later stages |
|-----------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **a. | **b. Manual removal of the protected attribute (race) only** – The data science team stripped the explicit “race” column but left all correlated proxies untouched, assuming that “removing the protected attribute” is sufficient for fairness. | This is the classic “fairness through unawareness” mistake; it does nothing to stop the model from exploiting proxies. | The model still produces disparate impact because the proxies act as stand‑ins for race. |
| **c. Aggressive dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) on all features** – The reduction mixed signals from both legitimate financial variables and the proxies, making it impossible to later separate “fair” from “unfair” components. | The transformation hid the source of bias, making post‑hoc debiasing far more difficult. | The downstream model cannot be inspected for fairness because the features are now opaque linear combinations. |

#### **Intervention Point #2 – Fair‑aware Feature Design**  
*What could have been done*:  

1. **Correlation analysis & removal of high‑risk proxies** – compute mutual information between each candidate feature and the protected attribute; drop or replace those above a pre‑set threshold (e.g., >0.2).  
2. **Use of *fair representations* (e.g., adversarial auto‑encoders)** – learn a latent space that maximally preserves predictive power while minimizing the ability of an adversary to recover race.  
3. **Domain‑expert review** – financial experts vet each engineered feature for *legitimacy* (e.g., “debt‑to‑income ratio” is legitimate; “average neighbourhood crime rate” is not).  

*Effect*: By eliminating or neutralizing proxies, the model would have far less capacity to encode race‑linked information, curbing disparate impact before training even begins.

---

| What actually happened | Why it mattered for bias | Causal link to later stages |
